sentences.chinese: 至元康末，婦人出兩襠，加乎交領之上，此內出外也。
sentences.literal: By the end of the Yuankang era, women wore the double-panel skirt outward, placing it above the overlapping collar—this was 'the inner emerging outward.'
sentences.idiomatic: Late in Yuankang, women reversed their skirts so the panels rode above the crossed collar—what should stay beneath showed on top.

sentences.chinese: 為車乘者苟貴輕細，又數變易其形，皆以白篾為純，蓋古喪車之遺象也。
sentences.literal: Those who fashioned carriages prized lightness and fineness, repeatedly altering their shapes, all using white bamboo splints for edging—likely a lingering likeness of ancient mourning carts.
sentences.idiomatic: Carriage-makers chased flimsy, ever-changing designs trimmed with white bamboo—echoes of funeral hearses from antiquity.

sentences.chinese: 夫乘者，君子之器。
sentences.literal: Now, riding is the instrument of the gentleman.
sentences.idiomatic: The carriage is the gentleman's proper equipage.

sentences.chinese: 蓋君子立心無恆，事不崇實也。
sentences.literal: For the gentleman sets his mind without constancy and does not honor substance in his affairs.
sentences.idiomatic: It matched gentlemen whose aims shifted and who prized display over substance.

sentences.chinese: 干寶以為晉之禍徵也。
sentences.literal: Gan Bao took it as an omen of calamity for Jin.
sentences.idiomatic: Gan Bao read it as a portent of Jin's ruin.

sentences.chinese: 及惠帝踐阼，權制在於寵臣，下掩上之應也。
sentences.literal: When Emperor Hui ascended the throne, controlling authority lay with favored ministers—the correspondence of 'below masking above.'
sentences.idiomatic: When Emperor Hui took the throne, power rested with favored courtiers—the pattern of inferiors overshadowing their sovereign.

sentences.chinese: 至永嘉末，六宮才人流冗沒于戎狄，內出外之應也。
sentences.literal: By the end of Yongjia, talented women of the six palaces drifted away and were lost among the Rong and Di—it was the correspondence of 'inner emerging outward.'
sentences.idiomatic: By Yongjia's end, palace ladies had scattered into barbarian hands—the inner court cast outward among outsiders.

sentences.chinese: 及天下撓亂，宰輔方伯多負其任，又數改易不崇實之應也。
sentences.literal: When all under heaven was thrown into turmoil, chief ministers and regional shepherds often betrayed their charges, and repeatedly altered offices without honoring substance—the correspondence thereof.
sentences.idiomatic: As the realm unraveled, ministers and governors failed their posts while titles changed without fixing anything—the omen of empty show.

sentences.chinese: 泰始之後，中國相尚用胡床貊槃，及為羌煮貊炙，貴人富室，必畜其器，吉享嘉會，皆以為先。
sentences.literal: After the Taishi era, the Central Lands came to esteem Hu benches and Mo trays, and to prepare Qiang-boil and Mo-roast dishes; the noble and wealthy kept such utensils ready, and at auspicious feasts and joyous gatherings they put them first.
sentences.idiomatic: After Taishi, Central Plains folk embraced alien benches and platters, Qiang-style boiled fare and roasted Mo dishes—the rich stocked them for every banquet.

sentences.chinese: 太康中，又以氈為絈頭及絡帶袴口。
sentences.literal: In the Taikang period, they further used felt for head-wraps and for belt bands and trouser cuffs.
sentences.idiomatic: By Taikang, felt wrapped the head, belt, and trouser legs—steppe style on the body.

sentences.chinese: 百姓相戲曰，中國必為胡所破。
sentences.literal: The common folk jested among themselves, saying the Central Lands would surely be broken by the Hu.
sentences.idiomatic: People joked that the heartland would fall to the steppe peoples.

sentences.chinese: 夫氈毳產于胡，而天下以為絈頭、帶身、袴口，胡既三制之矣，能無敗乎！
sentences.literal: Now felt and coarse wool are produced among the Hu, yet all under heaven used them for head-wraps, belts, and trouser cuffs—the Hu had already imposed three kinds of restraint; could there be no defeat!
sentences.idiomatic: Felt comes from the north, yet everyone wrapped head, waist, and ankles in it—the barbarians had claimed three garments off the body; defeat followed.

sentences.chinese: 至元康中，氐羌互反，永嘉後，劉、石遂篡中都，自後四夷迭據華土，是服妖之應也。
sentences.literal: By the Yuankang era, Di and Qiang rose against each other in turn; after Yongjia, Liu and Shi seized the central capital; thereafter the four Yi in succession occupied the Chinese soil—it was the correspondence of clothing prodigies.
sentences.idiomatic: Through Yuankang the Di and Qiang rebelled; after Yongjia Liu and Shi took Luoyang; then outsiders held the heartland—the 'ominous dress' omen fulfilled.

sentences.chinese: 初作屐者，婦人頭圓，男子頭方。
sentences.literal: When clogs were first made, women's toes were round, men's square.
sentences.idiomatic: Early clogs had round toes for women, square for men.

sentences.chinese: 圓者順之義，所以別男女也。
sentences.literal: Round means yielding; it served to distinguish male from female.
sentences.idiomatic: Round signified yielding—the line drawn between the sexes.

sentences.chinese: 至太康初，婦人屐乃頭方，與男無別。
sentences.literal: By early Taikang, women's clogs had square toes, no different from men's.
sentences.idiomatic: Come Taikang, women's clog toes went square like men's—the distinction blurred.

sentences.chinese: 此賈后專妒之徵也。
sentences.literal: This was an omen of Empress Jia's jealous monopoly.
sentences.idiomatic: It foretold Empress Jia's jealous grip on power.

sentences.chinese: 太康中，天下為《晉世寧》之舞，手接杯盤而反覆之，歌曰「晉世寧，舞杯盤」。
sentences.literal: In Taikang, all under heaven performed the dance of 'Jin at Peace,' catching cups and platters in the hands and flipping them, singing 'Jin at peace—dance with cups and platters.'
sentences.idiomatic: Taikang saw the 'Jin at Peace' dance—hands tossing cups and bowls while singers cried that peace in Jin meant spinning the cups.

sentences.chinese: 識者曰：「夫樂生人心，所以觀事也。
sentences.literal: Those who understood omens said: 'Music is born from the human heart; thereby one observes affairs.'
sentences.idiomatic: Critics said music springs from the heart and lays bare the age.

sentences.chinese: 今接杯盤於手上而反覆之，至危之事也。
sentences.literal: Now to catch cups and platters in the hands and flip them—this is an affair of utmost peril.
sentences.idiomatic: Juggling dishes in the hand is peril itself.

sentences.chinese: 杯盤者，酒食之器，而名曰《晉世寧》，言晉世之士苟偷於酒食之間，而知不及遠，晉世之寧猶杯盤之在手也。」
sentences.literal: Cups and platters are vessels for wine and food, yet the piece is named 'Jin at Peace'—it says the gentlemen of Jin sneak mere pleasure in wine and food, their knowledge reaching no farther; Jin's 'peace' is like cups and platters held in the hand.'
sentences.idiomatic: Cups mean feast and drink, yet the song promises peace—Jin's elite cared only for the banquet; their peace was as fragile as china in the palm.

sentences.chinese: 惠帝元康中，婦人之飾有五兵佩，又以金銀玳瑁之屬，為斧鉞戈戟，以當笄。
sentences.literal: In Emperor Hui's Yuankang era, women's ornaments included 'five-weapons' pendants; they further fashioned axes, halberds, spears, and ji from gold, silver, and tortoiseshell to serve as hairpins.
sentences.idiomatic: Yuankang ladies wore jewelry shaped like weapons—metal axes and halberds as hairpins.

sentences.chinese: 干寶以為「男女之別，國之大節，故服物異等，贄幣不同。
sentences.literal: Gan Bao thought: 'The distinction between man and woman is the great norm of the state; hence garments differ in grade and ritual offerings differ.'
sentences.idiomatic: Gan Bao: gender norms anchor the state—dress and ritual gifts must differ.

sentences.chinese: 今婦人而以兵器為飾，此婦人妖之甚者。
sentences.literal: Now for women to take weapons as ornaments—this is the utmost of feminine prodigy.
sentences.idiomatic: Arming women with ornaments was prodigy at its worst.

sentences.chinese: 於是遂有賈后之事」。
sentences.literal: Thereupon there came the affair of Empress Jia.'
sentences.idiomatic: Then came Empress Jia's coup against the heir.

sentences.chinese: 終亡天下。
sentences.literal: In the end the realm perished.
sentences.idiomatic: The dynasty fell.

sentences.chinese: 是時婦人結髮者既成，以繒急束其環，名曰擷子紒。
sentences.literal: At this time, among women who bound their hair, once the arrangement was complete, they tightly bound the coil with silk and called it the 'plucked-child knot.'
sentences.idiomatic: Women finished their coifs, then cinched them tight with silk—the 'plucked-child bun.'

sentences.chinese: 始自中宮，天下化之。
sentences.literal: It began in the inner palace; all under heaven imitated it.
sentences.idiomatic: The palace set the fashion; the realm copied it.

sentences.chinese: 其後賈后廢害太子之應也。
sentences.literal: Afterward it corresponded to Empress Jia's deposition and murder of the heir apparent.
sentences.idiomatic: It matched Empress Jia's destruction of the crown prince.

sentences.chinese: 元康中，天下始相傚為烏杖以柱掖，其後稍施其鐓，住則植之。
sentences.literal: In Yuankang, all under heaven began to imitate crow-headed staffs braced under the arm; later they gradually fitted ferrules, and when resting planted them upright.
sentences.idiomatic: Yuankang folk copied crow-head staffs tucked under the arm—later capped with metal ferrules and planted like poles when idle.

sentences.chinese: 夫木，東方之行，金之臣也。
sentences.literal: Wood is the phase of the east; it is subject to metal.
sentences.idiomatic: Wood belongs to the east; it yields to metal.

sentences.chinese: 杖者扶體之器，烏其頭者，尤便用也。
sentences.literal: The staff is an instrument to support the body; crowning it with a crow's head makes it especially handy.
sentences.idiomatic: A staff steadies the walker; a crow tip made it handier.

sentences.chinese: 必旁柱掖者，旁救之象也。
sentences.literal: That it must brace under the arm—this is an image of rescue from the side.
sentences.idiomatic: Tucking it under the arm suggested sidelong rescue.

sentences.chinese: 施其金，柱則植之，言木因于金，能孤立也。
sentences.literal: They fitted its metal; braced on the staff it stands planted—it says wood depends on metal and can stand alone.
sentences.idiomatic: Metal ferrules let the planted staff stand—wood leaning on metal yet standing alone.

sentences.chinese: 及懷湣之世，王室多故，而此中都喪敗，元帝以籓臣樹德東方，維持天下，柱掖之應也。
sentences.literal: By the reigns of Emperors Huai and Min, the royal house suffered many crises and the central capital fell; Emperor Yuan, a feudal prince, planted virtue in the east and upheld all under heaven—the correspondence of bracing under the arm.
sentences.idiomatic: When Luoyang fell, Yuan as prince raised the east—exactly the 'underarm brace' sign.

sentences.chinese: 至社稷無主，海內歸之，遂承天命，建都江外，獨立之應也。
sentences.literal: When altars had no master and the realm turned to him, he received Heaven's mandate, founded the capital south of the Yangtze, and stood alone—the correspondence thereof.
sentences.idiomatic: When nothing held the center, the realm rallied south—the sign of standing alone became court.

sentences.chinese: 元康、太安之間，江淮之域有敗屩自聚於道，多者至四五十量，人或散投坑穀，明日視之復如故。
sentences.literal: Between Yuankang and Tai'an, in the Jiang-Huai region worn sandals piled of themselves on the roads—sometimes forty or fifty pairs; people might scatter them into pits and valleys, yet next morning they were as before.
sentences.idiomatic: Yuankang–Tai'an: tattered sandals heaped on Jiang-Huai roads—scatter them at night, they reappeared by dawn.

sentences.chinese: 或云，見狸銜聚之。
sentences.literal: Some said they saw foxes gather them in their mouths.
sentences.idiomatic: Some swore foxes stacked them.

sentences.chinese: 干寶以為'夫屩者，人之賤服，處於勞辱，黔庶之象也。
sentences.literal: Gan Bao thought: 'Sandals are the mean clothing of men; they dwell in toil and shame—the image of the black-haired populace.'
sentences.idiomatic: Gan Bao: sandals are laborers' shoes—the common folk in grime.

sentences.chinese: 敗者，疲弊之象；
sentences.literal: 'Tattered' is the image of exhaustion;
sentences.idiomatic: 'Worn' meant spent strength.

sentences.chinese: 道者，四方往來，所以交通王命也。
sentences.literal: 'Road' is where the four quarters come and go—thereby the king's commands travel.
sentences.idiomatic: Roads carry the king's orders.

sentences.chinese: 今敗屩聚於道者，象黔庶罷病，將相聚為亂，以絕王命也」。
sentences.literal: 'Now worn sandals pile on the roads—it images the black-haired folk weary and sick, about to gather in rebellion and cut off the king's command.'
sentences.idiomatic: Sandals heaped on highways meant exhausted masses rising to sever the throne.

sentences.chinese: 太安中，發壬午兵，百姓怨叛。
sentences.literal: In Tai'an they levied the ren-wu army; the hundred surnames resented and rebelled.
sentences.idiomatic: Tai'an's ren-wu draft drove commoners to revolt.

sentences.chinese: 江夏張昌唱亂，荊楚從之如流。
sentences.literal: Zhang Chang of Jiangxia raised rebellion; Jing and Chu followed like flowing water.
sentences.idiomatic: Zhang Chang rose in Jiangxia; Jing-Chu rushed to join him.

sentences.chinese: 於是兵革歲起，服妖也。
sentences.literal: Thereupon arms rose year after year—a clothing prodigy.
sentences.idiomatic: War followed yearly—the dress omen fulfilled.

sentences.chinese: 初，魏造白帢，橫縫其前以別後，名之曰顏帢，傳行之。
sentences.literal: At first Wei made white kerchiefs, sewing the front crosswise to distinguish back from front; they called them 'face kerchiefs' and handed them down.
sentences.idiomatic: Wei issued white caps with a cross seam front-to-back—the 'face kerchief.'

sentences.chinese: 至永嘉之間，稍去其縫，名無顏帢，而婦人束發，其緩彌甚，紒之堅不能自立，發被於額，目出而已。
sentences.literal: By Yongjia they gradually removed the seam—called 'no-face kerchiefs'; women's hair bun bindings grew ever looser; the knot could not stand on its own; hair draped over the forehead until only the eyes showed.
sentences.idiomatic: Yongjia dropped the seam—'faceless' caps—and women's buns went slack, hair falling past brows.

sentences.chinese: 無顏者，愧之言也。
sentences.literal: 'No face' is language of shame.
sentences.idiomatic: 'No face' spoke of shame.

sentences.chinese: 覆額者，慚之貌也。
sentences.literal: 'Covering the forehead' is the appearance of remorse.
sentences.idiomatic: Hair masking the brow looked like hiding one's face in guilt.

sentences.chinese: 其緩彌甚者，言天下亡禮與義，放縱情性，及其終極，至於大恥也。
sentences.literal: That the looseness grew extreme speaks of all under heaven losing ritual and rightness, indulging nature to the utmost, reaching great shame.
sentences.idiomatic: The ever-looser binding meant ritual collapsed and appetite ran to utter disgrace.

sentences.chinese: 永嘉之後，二帝不反，天下愧焉。
sentences.literal: After Yongjia, the two emperors did not return; all under heaven was shamed.
sentences.idiomatic: After Yongjia two emperors never came home—the realm hung its head.

sentences.chinese: 孝懷帝永嘉中，士大夫競服生箋單衣。
sentences.literal: Under Emperor Huai of Jin's Yongjia era, gentlemen competed to wear raw paper single robes.
sentences.idiomatic: Yongjia scholars vied to wear stiff raw-paper robes.

sentences.chinese: 識者指之曰：「此則古者繐衰，諸侯所以服天子也。
sentences.literal: Those who understood pointed and said: 'This is like the ancient cui straw mourning—what feudal lords wore for the Son of Heaven.'
sentences.idiomatic: Critics pointed: that's cui mourning straw—what lords wear for the Son of Heaven.

sentences.chinese: 今無故服之，殆有應乎！
sentences.literal: Now to wear it without cause—perhaps there is a correspondence!
sentences.idiomatic: With no bereavement? A bad sign.

sentences.chinese: 」其後遂有胡賊之亂，帝遇害焉。
sentences.literal: ' Thereafter came the turmoil of Hu bandits, and the emperor was murdered thereby.
sentences.idiomatic: Then barbarian armies rose and killed the emperor.

sentences.chinese: 元帝太興中，兵士以絳囊縛紒。
sentences.literal: In Emperor Yuan's Daxing era, soldiers bound their topknots with crimson pouches.
sentences.idiomatic: Daxing troops tied topknots in red silk bags.

sentences.chinese: 識者曰：「紒者在首，為乾，君道也。
sentences.literal: Those who understood said: 'The topknot is on the head—it is Qian, the way of the lord.'
sentences.idiomatic: Critics: the bun crowns the head—Qian, the ruler.

sentences.chinese: 囊者坤，臣道也。
sentences.literal: 'The pouch is Kun—the way of the minister.'
sentences.idiomatic: The bag is Kun—the minister.

sentences.chinese: 今以硃囊縛紒，臣道上侵君之象也。
sentences.literal: 'Now to bind the topknot with a vermilion pouch—it is the image of the minister's way encroaching on the lord.'
sentences.idiomatic: Red sack on the ruler's knot—ministers climbing past their lord.

sentences.chinese: 」於是王敦陵上焉。
sentences.literal: ' Thereupon Wang Dun lorded over his sovereign.
sentences.idiomatic: Then Wang Dun bullied the throne.

sentences.chinese: 舊為羽扇柄者，刻木象其骨形，列羽用十，取全數也。
sentences.literal: Formerly feather-fan handles were carved in wood like bone pattern; they arrayed ten feathers—taking the complete number.
sentences.idiomatic: Old feather fans used ten plumes—the full count.

sentences.chinese: 自中興初，王敦南征，始改為長柄，下出可捉，而減其羽用八。
sentences.literal: From the first restoration, when Wang Dun campaigned south, they began to make long handles extending below for gripping, and reduced the feathers to eight.
sentences.idiomatic: After the court fled south, Wang Dun's campaign brought long handles and cut feathers to eight.

sentences.chinese: 識者尤之曰：「夫羽扇，翼之名也。
sentences.literal: Those who understood faulted it, saying: 'The feather fan—the name of wings.'
sentences.idiomatic: Critics: feathers mean wings.

sentences.chinese: 創為長柄者，將執其柄以制羽翼也。
sentences.literal: 'To invent a long handle is to grasp the handle and control the wings.'
sentences.idiomatic: A long shaft means seizing the haft to master the wings.

sentences.chinese: 改十為八者，將未備奪已備也。
sentences.literal: 'To change ten to eight is to take from what is not yet ready what is already ready.'
sentences.idiomatic: Ten cut to eight—strip the prepared of their surplus.

sentences.chinese: 此殆敦之擅權以制朝廷之柄，又將以無德之材欲竊非據也。
sentences.literal: 'This is likely Wang Dun's usurping authority to control the court's handle, and moreover intending with talent without virtue to steal a seat not his own.'
sentences.idiomatic: It foretold Wang Dun grabbing the reins—unworthy talent eyeing the throne.

sentences.chinese: 」是時，為衣者又上短，帶才至於掖，著帽者又以帶縛項。
sentences.literal: ' At that time, those who made garments made the upper short; sashes reached only to the armpit; those who wore caps further bound the neck with the sash.
sentences.idiomatic: Meanwhile jackets shrank, belts barely reached the armpit, hat strings choked the neck.

sentences.chinese: 下逼上，上無地也。
sentences.literal: Below pressing above; above there is no ground.
sentences.idiomatic: Below crowding above—the ruler had nowhere to stand.

sentences.chinese: 為袴者直幅為口，無殺，下大之象。
sentences.literal: Those who made trousers used straight panels for the mouth, without taper—an image of large below.
sentences.idiomatic: Trousers went straight-cut and baggy below—the top-heavy omen.

sentences.chinese: 尋而王敦謀逆，再攻京師。
sentences.literal: Soon Wang Dun plotted rebellion and twice attacked the capital.
sentences.idiomatic: Soon Wang Dun rebelled and struck the capital twice.

sentences.chinese: 海西嗣位，忘設豹尾。
sentences.literal: When Prince Hai of the West succeeded, he forgot to set out the leopard tail.
sentences.idiomatic: When Emperor Hai ascended, he omitted the leopard-tail insignia.

sentences.chinese: 天戒若曰，夫豹尾，儀服之主，大人所以豹變也。
sentences.literal: Heaven's warning seemed to say: the leopard tail is master of ceremonial dress—by it great men 'leopard-transform.'
sentences.idiomatic: Heaven warned: the leopard tail crowns ritual dress—the great man's transformation.

sentences.chinese: 而海西豹變之日，非所宜忘而忘之。
sentences.literal: Yet on the day Prince Hai 'leopard-transformed,' what ought not be forgotten was forgotten.
sentences.idiomatic: Yet on the day he should transform, he forgot the very emblem.

sentences.chinese: 非主社稷之人，故忘其豹尾，示不終也。
sentences.literal: He is not one to master the altars; hence he forgot his leopard tail—it showed he would not last.
sentences.idiomatic: No true steward of the realm—forgot the tail; doomed not to endure.

sentences.chinese: 尋而被廢焉。
sentences.literal: Soon he was deposed.
sentences.idiomatic: He was deposed soon after.

sentences.chinese: 孝武太元中，人不復著帩頭。
sentences.literal: Under Emperor Xiaowu's Taiyuan era, people no longer wore forehead kerchiefs.
sentences.idiomatic: Taiyuan folk quit wearing forehead cloths.

sentences.chinese: 天戒若曰，頭者元首，帩者助元首為儀飾者也。
sentences.literal: Heaven's warning seemed to say: the head is the sovereign element; the kerchief assists the head as adornment.
sentences.idiomatic: Heaven: the head is supreme; the kerchief aids it as ornament.

sentences.chinese: 今忽廢之，若人君獨立無輔佐，以至危亡也。
sentences.literal: Now suddenly to discard it is like the lord standing alone without assistants, unto peril and ruin.
sentences.idiomatic: To shed it was like a ruler bereft of ministers—hurtling toward ruin.

sentences.chinese: 至安帝，桓玄乃篡位焉。
sentences.literal: By Emperor An, Huan Xuan then usurped the throne.
sentences.idiomatic: Come Emperor An, Huan Xuan seized the throne.

sentences.chinese: 舊為屐者，齒皆達楄上，名曰露卯。
sentences.literal: Formerly clogs had teeth reaching onto the upper—called 'exposed mao.'
sentences.idiomatic: Old clogs had pegs showing above the vamp—'bright mao.'

sentences.chinese: 太元中忽不徹，名日陰卯。
sentences.literal: In Taiyuan they suddenly did not penetrate through—called 'hidden mao.'
sentences.idiomatic: Taiyuan suddenly hid the pegs—'dark mao.' (Graph 名日 for 名曰.)

sentences.chinese: 識者以為卯，謀也，必有陰謀之事。
sentences.literal: Those who understood thought mao means 'plot'—there must be matters of secret plotting.
sentences.idiomatic: Critics: mao puns with 'plot'—conspiracy ahead.

sentences.chinese: 至烈宗末，驃騎參軍袁悅之始攬構內外，隆安中遂謀詐相傾，以致大亂。
sentences.literal: By the end of Emperor Liezong, Cavalry Adjutant Yuan Yuezhi first wove intrigue inside and outside; in Long'an he then plotted fraud and mutual toppling, bringing great turmoil.
sentences.idiomatic: Late Liezong, Yuan Yuezhi spun palace intrigue; Long'an brought coups and chaos.

sentences.chinese: 太元中，公主婦女必緩鬢傾髻，以為盛飾。
sentences.literal: In Taiyuan, princesses and women invariably loosened their sideburn locks and tilted their chignons, deeming it grand adornment.
sentences.idiomatic: Taiyuan noblewomen wore loose side hair and slanted buns as high fashion.

sentences.chinese: 用髲既多，不可恆戴，乃先於木及籠上裝之，名曰假髻，或名假頭。
sentences.literal: Because supplementary hairpieces were many and could not always be worn, they first mounted them on wood and cages—called false chignon, or false head.
sentences.idiomatic: Heavy hairpieces could not be worn daily—they mounted them on frames first, 'wig-head.'

sentences.chinese: 至於貧家，不能自辦，自號無頭，就人借頭。
sentences.literal: As for poor households that could not supply them, they called themselves 'without heads' and borrowed heads from others.
sentences.idiomatic: Poor families called themselves 'headless' and borrowed wigs.

sentences.chinese: 遂布天下，亦服妖也。
sentences.literal: It spread through all under heaven—again a clothing prodigy.
sentences.idiomatic: The fad spread—a dress omen again.

sentences.chinese: 無幾時，孝武晏駕而天下騷動，刑戮無數，多喪其元。
sentences.literal: Before long, Emperor Xiaowu died in his carriage and all under heaven was in turmoil; executions were countless, many losing their heads.
sentences.idiomatic: Soon Emperor Xiaowu died; the realm erupted in executions and decapitations.

sentences.chinese: 至於大殮，皆刻木及蠟或縛菰草為頭，是假頭之應云。
sentences.literal: When it came to laying out for burial, all carved wood and wax or bound rush grass for heads—this was the correspondence of the false head, it is said.
sentences.idiomatic: Come burial, families carved wood, wax, or rush heads—the false-head omen fulfilled.

sentences.chinese: 桓玄篡立，殿上施絳帳，鏤黃金為顏，四角金龍銜五色羽葆流蘇。
sentences.literal: When Huan Xuan usurped, he hung crimson curtains in the hall, chased gold for borders; golden dragons at the four corners held five-colored feather plumes and tassels.
sentences.idiomatic: Huan Xuan's usurpation brought scarlet hall drapes, gold fretwork, dragons at corners trailing colored plumes.

sentences.chinese: 群下相謂曰：「頗類轜車。
sentences.literal: The assembled ministers said to one another: 'Rather like a bier hearse.'
sentences.idiomatic: Courtiers whispered: looks like a funeral hearse.

sentences.chinese: 」尋而玄敗，此服之妖也。
sentences.literal: ' Soon Huan Xuan was defeated—this was prodigy in dress.
sentences.idiomatic: Huan fell soon after—a costume prodigy.

sentences.chinese: 晉末皆冠小而衣裳博大，風流相放，輿臺成俗。
sentences.literal: At Jin's end all wore small caps but vast robes and skirts; they copied one another in elegance until even grooms and runners made it custom.
sentences.idiomatic: Late Jin: tiny caps, billowing robes—fashion aped even by servants.

sentences.chinese: 識者曰：「上小而下大，此禪代之象也。
sentences.literal: Those who understood said: 'Small above and large below—this is the image of abdication and replacement.'
sentences.idiomatic: Critics: small top, big bottom—the abdication sign.

sentences.chinese: 」尋而宋受終焉。
sentences.literal: ' Soon Song received the abdication and ended [Jin].'
sentences.idiomatic: Song took the mandate soon after.
— (editorial break before the subsection on fowl prodigies.)

sentences.chinese: 雞禍
sentences.literal: Chicken calamities.
sentences.idiomatic: Chicken Omens

sentences.chinese: =魏明帝，廷尉府中雌雞化為雄，不鳴不將。
sentences.literal: = Wei Mingdi—in the Minister of Justice compound a hen turned into a cock; it did not crow and did not lead.
sentences.idiomatic: Wei Mingdi: in the Court of Justice yard a hen became a rooster—it did not crow and did not lead the flock.

sentences.chinese: 干寶曰：「是歲宣帝平遼東，百姓始有與能之義，此其象也。
sentences.literal: Gan Bao said: 'That year Emperor Xuan pacified Liaodong; the hundred surnames first had the sense of yielding to the capable—this was its image
sentences.idiomatic: Gan Bao: that year the court pacified Liaodong and the people learned to yield to the worthy—that matched one half of the sign;

sentences.chinese: 然晉三后並以人臣終，不鳴不將，又天意也。」
sentences.literal: yet the three later Jin empresses all ended as subjects—neither crowing nor leading—again Heaven's intent.'
sentences.idiomatic: yet three Jin empresses all ended as mere subjects—still silent, still not leading: Heaven's intent again.
